Hermas
HER-mas
proper noun
A Greek name, a contracted form (as of Hermodorus or Hermogenes), bearing the element Hermes, the name of a pagan messenger-god.

See also: Hermas

📖 Biblical Definition

Hermas is a believer of the Roman church greeted by Paul: “Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren which are with them” (Rom 16:14). He is named in a group of five men, set just before another saint called Hermes, both names sharing the same pagan root yet borne now by men in Christ. Of this Hermas the inspired record tells us nothing beyond the greeting; his labours and his end are unknown to us. An ancient tradition has sought to identify this Hermas with the author of the second-century work “The Shepherd of Hermas,” and Origen and others entertained the link; but this rests on no solid ground, the dates strain against it, and we ought not build doctrine or biography upon a guess. The Hermas of this entry is simply the disciple at Rome whom Paul loved and saluted, one of the “brethren which are with them” in a household of the faith. His worth lies not in any deed history records but in his union with Christ. The Spirit set his name in Scripture, and that is honour beyond the reach of fame. Like his fellows in this list, he stands for the great company of ordinary saints whom God numbers, names, and keeps to the end.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A Christian at Rome greeted by Paul in Romans 16; not to be confidently identified with the later writer of “The Shepherd.”

expand to see more

HERMAS, a believer in the church at Rome saluted by the apostle Paul.

Named in a group of five with Asyncritus, Phlegon, Patrobas, and Hermes (Rom 16:14).

His Greek name carries the element Hermes, a pagan messenger-god.

An ancient tradition links him to the later “Shepherd of Hermas,” though without firm ground.

Scripture records nothing of his life beyond the greeting.

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 16:14 — "Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren which are with them."

Rom 16:16 — "Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you."

1Co 1:26 — "For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called:"

Rev 3:5 — "He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The danger of building biography on tradition rather than the sober witness of Scripture.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Hermas is restraint where Scripture is silent. The hasty identification of this man with the author of “The Shepherd” warns us not to dress a bare name in a borrowed history; we honour the Word by holding to what it says and no more.

His honour, like that of his fellows, lies wholly in being known to Christ. The disciple at Rome teaches us that fame is nothing and union with the Saviour is everything. The Lord will not blot out the name of him that overcometh, and that promise covers every obscure saint whom the world never knew.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

A contracted Greek personal name built on the root Hermes, common among freedmen.

expand to see more

Hermas — a shortened Greek name, as of Hermodorus or Hermogenes.

It carries the element Hermes, the name of a pagan messenger-deity.

Such names were frequent among slaves and freedmen of imperial Rome.

It stands just before the kindred name Hermes in the same verse.

It is distinct from the second-century work “The Shepherd of Hermas.”

Usage

"Paul greeted Hermas as one of the brethren at Rome."

"We must not confound the Hermas of Romans 16 with a later writer."

"Hermas is honoured by a single mention in the inspired Word."
